title: The six components
point: The model proposes and the orchestrator decides; each of the six components keeps one invariant that the others rely on.
definition: A production agent splits into six components: orchestrator, reasoning model, tool gateway, memory, guardrails and observability. Each owns one invariant, so any failure can be traced to the component whose invariant broke.

objective.text: Given an incident description, identify which of the six components owned the broken invariant and state the check that would have caught it.

misconceptions.claim: The model executes a tool when it emits a tool call.
misconceptions.correction: The model only returns a proposal. The orchestrator decides whether to act, and the tool gateway authorises, validates and executes the call.

misconceptions.claim: Guardrails can check the budget after the model call returns.
misconceptions.correction: A check after the call cannot prevent the spend it is meant to cap. Guardrails check the projected cost before each call and downgrade or halt on a violation.

l1: Orchestrator: every run terminates and emits a trace. Reasoning model: returns a proposal, and nothing it says executes by itself. The model proposes, the orchestrator decides.
Tool gateway: an allowlist per principal, schema validation, a timeout and a typed result. Authorisation runs before validation, so a denied caller never learns the tool's schema.

Memory: reads are bounded, every item carries its source, and scope to the user is enforced in the store. Guardrails: a violation downgrades or halts the run, and the budget is checked before each call.
Observability: one span per step, carrying tokens and cost, so any run can be reconstructed after the fact.
l2: A user reports that the assistant quoted another customer's order. The trace shows memory returned an item with no user scope. The broken invariant belongs to memory: scope must be enforced in the store, not in the prompt.

A second incident: a run spent $4 on a task capped at $0.50. The guardrail checked spend after each call, so the expensive call had already happened. The fix is to check projected cost before the call.
In both cases the trace from observability is what made the diagnosis possible. Without one span per step, you would be guessing.
l3: Enforcing user scope in the store costs an index and a filter on every read. Enforcing it in the prompt costs nothing, but it fails on the first successful prompt injection.
Put numbers on it: a scoped read might add 2 ms to a 1,500 ms step, about 0.13 per cent. That is a cheap price for an invariant that no prompt can talk its way around.
The general rule: place each invariant in the component that can enforce it mechanically, and never rely on the model to keep it.
